title: LFU Cache — HashMap + frequency map + LinkedHashSet.
shortTitle: LFU Cache — HashMap plus frequency map plus LinkedHashSet buckets

s1_definition.profdef: An LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry with the lowest access count when it is full, and breaks ties by evicting the least recently used among the lowest-frequency entries. The O(1) design keeps a key-to-value-and-frequency map, a frequency-to-keys map where each bucket is a LinkedHashSet preserving insertion order for tie-breaking, and a running minimum-frequency counter so eviction knows exactly which bucket to pull from.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only a few customer files on the desk, and instead of keeping the ones touched most recently, the rule is to keep the ones touched the most times overall. Each file has a tally mark for every time it is used. When the desk is full and a new file arrives, the file with the fewest tally marks is archived, and if several files are tied on the fewest marks, the one that has sat untouched the longest among them goes first.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track each key's frequency, group keys into frequency buckets of insertion order, and keep a minimum-frequency pointer so the least-used, oldest-tied entry is evicted in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry with the lowest access count when it is full, and breaks ties by evicting the least recently used among the lowest-frequency entries. The O(1) design keeps a key-to-value-and-frequency map, a frequency-to-keys map where each bucket is a LinkedHashSet preserving insertion order for tie-breaking, and a running minimum-frequency counter so eviction knows exactly which bucket to pull from.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only a few customer files on the desk, and instead of keeping the ones touched most recently, the rule is to keep the ones touched the most times overall. Each file has a tally mark for every time it is used. When the desk is full and a new file arrives, the file with the fewest tally marks is archived, and if several files are tied on the fewest marks, the one that has sat untouched the longest among them goes first.

**One line to remember:** Track each key's frequency, group keys into frequency buckets of insertion order, and keep a minimum-frequency pointer so the least-used, oldest-tied entry is evicted in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The cache stores three structures. The first is a map from key to a small holder of the value and the current frequency. The second is a map from a frequency number to a LinkedHashSet of keys that currently have that frequency; the LinkedHashSet matters because it remembers insertion order, which gives the least-recently-used tie-break for free. The third is a single integer, the minimum frequency currently present.

On a `get(key)`, if the key is missing we return a miss. If present, we read the value and then promote its frequency: we remove the key from its current frequency bucket, increment its frequency, and add it to the next bucket. If the bucket we emptied was the minimum frequency and it is now empty, we increment the minimum frequency, because no key has that old frequency anymore.

On a `put(key, value)`, if the key exists we update the value and promote its frequency exactly like a get. If the key is new and the cache is at capacity, we first evict: we go to the minimum-frequency bucket, remove the first key in that LinkedHashSet (the oldest among the least frequent), and delete it from the value map. Then we insert the new key with frequency one, add it to the frequency-one bucket, and reset the minimum frequency to one because the newest entry always starts at frequency one.

Every operation is O(1) because the maps give direct access and LinkedHashSet add and remove are constant time. A senior nuance: resetting the minimum frequency to one on every new insertion is correct precisely because a fresh key has frequency one, which is the smallest possible. Another nuance is that the LinkedHashSet, not a plain HashSet, is required to get deterministic least-recently-used tie-breaking.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India caches exchange-rate lookups. Some currency pairs are queried constantly all day while others are queried rarely. When the cache is full, the right thing to evict is the pair that has been looked up the fewest times overall, not merely the one touched least recently, because a steadily popular pair should survive a brief burst of rare lookups.

This is exactly how an LFU cache works. The entry with the lowest total access count is evicted first.

Problem 2 — When several rarely used pairs are tied at the same low frequency, we still need a deterministic, fair rule for which one leaves, and it should be the one that has gone cold the longest.

This is exactly why each frequency bucket is a LinkedHashSet, so the oldest key among the tied-lowest frequency is removed first.

The code will have an `Entry` holder class, an `LfuCache` class with the three structures, and a runnable demo that exercises hits that change frequencies and triggers an LFU eviction with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cache of capacity 2 and a sequence of puts and gets on currency pairs.

Step 1: `put("USD-INR", 8325)` inserts USD-INR with frequency one, places it in bucket one, and sets the minimum frequency to one.

Step 2: `put("EUR-INR", 9010)` inserts EUR-INR with frequency one, placing it in bucket one after USD-INR. The minimum frequency stays one.

Step 3: `get("USD-INR")` reads the value and promotes USD-INR: it is removed from bucket one and added to bucket two. Bucket one still holds EUR-INR, so the minimum frequency stays one. A second `get("USD-INR")` promotes it again to bucket three.

Step 4: `put("GBP-INR", 10550)` is a new key and the cache is at capacity. The minimum-frequency bucket is bucket one, holding only EUR-INR, so EUR-INR is evicted and logged. GBP-INR is inserted into bucket one, and the minimum frequency resets to one.

Step 5: `get("EUR-INR")` misses because it was evicted. `get("USD-INR")` and `get("GBP-INR")` both hit.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get USD-INR -> 8325
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get USD-INR -> 8325
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    EVICT EUR-INR (freq 1)
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get EUR-INR -> null
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get USD-INR -> 8325
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get GBP-INR -> 10550
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An LFU cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry with the lowest access count when it needs room, and when several entries tie at the lowest count it evicts the one that has been untouched the longest among them. The difference from an LRU cache is that LRU cares only about recency while LFU cares about total usage, so a steadily popular entry survives a short burst of rare lookups.

I implement it with three structures that together give constant-time operations. The first is a map from each key to a holder of its value and its current frequency. The second is a map from a frequency number to a LinkedHashSet of the keys at that frequency, and I use a LinkedHashSet specifically because it preserves insertion order, which gives me a clean least-recently-used tie-break among entries of equal frequency. The third is a single integer that tracks the current minimum frequency so eviction knows exactly which bucket to pull from.

On every access I promote the key by removing it from its current frequency bucket, incrementing its frequency, and adding it to the next bucket, and if I just emptied the minimum-frequency bucket I bump the minimum. On a new insertion when the cache is full, I evict the first key in the minimum-frequency bucket, which is the oldest among the least frequent, then insert the new key at frequency one and reset the minimum frequency to one, which is correct because a brand new key always starts at the smallest possible frequency.

In my project at National Bank of India, we cached foreign-exchange rate lookups where some currency pairs were queried constantly while others were queried rarely, and when the cache filled we wanted to drop the least-queried pair rather than merely the least-recently-touched one. The LFU design kept the consistently popular pairs resident even during bursts of rare queries, and the LinkedHashSet buckets gave us a fair, deterministic rule for breaking ties among the cold pairs.
